page.text:
Now we have the start of an (incomplete) definition of a set which is an
abstract concept. By that I mean, a "set" is a name describing a whole
collection of concrete objects that are each "sets". `Describes:` is
the mechanism to describe such a type.

A concrete object, on the other hand, is a specific instance of an type
and a `Defines:` is used to define such concrete instances.

For example, we can define the specific set, the empty set.

```mlg
[\empty.set]
Defines: X is \set
expresses:
. not:
  . exists: Y is \set
    suchThat: Y "in" X
Documented:
. called: "empty set"
. written: "\emptyset"
Id: "96908ddf-5fc5-455d-9cfd-eaf0fd6ada38"
```

Here `\empty.set` is the identifier for an empty set, and the `Defines: X
is \set` section specifies that `X` is the interal symbol that represents
the empty set and that an empty set is a set.

Next the `expresses:` section defines the characteristics of the empty
set, i.e. it is a set that contains no other sets, and again we document
how the empty set is spoken and written.
